text: A ServiceNow Developer's day-to-day centers on extending what the out-of-box platform can do, inside a scoped application. Course 6 walked through building exactly this: custom tables, forms, and the scripts that drive their behavior. In a real job, you're usually doing this against a specific request — build an internal tool for tracking equipment loans, or add a custom approval step the default workflow can't handle.
That request becomes a scoped application: custom tables and forms, Business Rules and Script Includes carrying the logic, and a Service Portal widget for the piece end users actually see.

Four building blocks fill most of the actual sprint. Business Rules are server-side scripts that run on insert, update, delete, or query — the backbone of most custom logic. Script Includes are reusable server-side libraries called from those rules so logic isn't copy-pasted everywhere; course 5 built the JavaScript fundamentals, and course 6 applied them here. Client Scripts run in the browser, controlling form behavior in real time. And Service Portal widgets combine server-side data with a front-end template for the pages end users actually see. Course 7 adds the integration layer on top — pulling and pushing data to outside systems is routine now, not a specialty.

Here's the honest distinction worth understanding before you apply. A ServiceNow Developer is rarely standing up their own servers or choosing a database engine — the platform already provides the data layer, the UI framework, the workflow engine, and the hosting. The real skill is building correctly within that framework: knowing when a Business Rule is the right tool versus a Client Script, and how to extend a scoped application without fighting the platform's own conventions. That matters directly in an interview, too — naming these specific building blocks demonstrates real platform fluency, versus a generic "I'm a developer" answer that signals a possible gap.
